title: Bless the Lord, O my soul (Psalm 103)
hookLine: he knows our frame; he remembers we are dust

lines: A NUDGE TO YOUR OWN SOUL.
cards: Memory is strangely lopsided. A teacher's sharp comment in seventh grade: still there, word for word, decades later. The stranger who held a door when your arms were full of groceries last Tuesday: gone by Wednesday.

Memory keeps the wounds on file and lets the kindnesses slip through. It isn't a moral failing exactly; memory seems to keep watch for threats. But left alone, it can make a life look harder than it was.
Psalm one hundred three opens with a person giving their own soul a firm reminder, almost a nudge in the ribs. Don't forget.

teach.b: Psalm one hundred three begins, in the King James Bible: "Bless the LORD, O my soul: and all that is within me, bless his holy name. Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits."
Like the deer psalm, the writer is talking to himself. But this time it isn't comfort. It's a reminder.
Then he counts the benefits out loud, one after another: who forgives, who heals, who redeems your life from destruction, who crowns you with lovingkindness, who renews your youth like the eagle's.
And this psalm doesn't ask for anything. No request, no complaint, from beginning to end. It just remembers.

teach.h: AS FAR AS EAST FROM WEST
teach.b: "As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us." East and west never meet; you can travel east forever.

"Like as a father pitieth his children, so the LORD pitieth them that fear him. For he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust." Frame is how a person is put together, what they're made of.
God knows people are breakable, the psalm says, and is gentle about it. Human days are like grass: the wind passes over, and the place forgets them.
And then the turn: "But the mercy of the LORD is from everlasting to everlasting."
People forget. God remembers that we are dust, and remembers mercy. By the end the psalm calls on the angels, every work of God, and finally its own soul again.
Henry Francis Lyte turned it into a hymn, Praise, My Soul, the King of Heaven, and churches still sing it.

how: Many Christians pray Psalm 103 as a prayer of thanksgiving, and it is sung in hymns such as Henry Francis Lyte's "Praise, My Soul, the King of Heaven."

o: loyal, tender love that God crowns a life with
a kind word spoken to a lonely friend
a warm feeling toward strangers you meet

games.q: what's inside the psalm — tap the pairs.
p: as far as the east is from the west
how far our sins are removed
Praise, My Soul, the King of Heaven

s: Psalm 103 is full of requests to God
it asks for nothing. it remembers, from start to finish.
the psalm says God remembers we are dust
"for he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust."
the psalm writer speaks to his own soul

games.q: you've just told your soul to bless the Lord. what does the psalm do next?
o: ask for a long list of things.
count, one by one, what has already been given.
games.why: it lists the benefits: who forgiveth, who healeth, who redeemeth, who crowneth. the whole psalm asks for nothing.

practice: Find three specific benefits you've received, not big abstract ones: a meal someone cooked, a body that got you out of bed, a friend who texted back. Say each one quietly, the way the psalm counts them, and sit with the list.
If you pray, say the line, bless the Lord, O my soul; if you don't, let the three things sit there, remembered on purpose.

wordCard.voice: Lovingkindness. One of the benefits this psalm says God crowns us with, along with forgiveness, healing and a youth renewed like the eagle's.

orig.note: Hebrew: bless, my soul. the psalm's opening command, spoken to the writer's own self.

carryVoice: Your line: forget not all his benefits. Wounds stay on file by themselves; kindnesses need a reminder. See you tomorrow.
